tasks.task_description: Build the ball-passing network for the Huskies from passingevents.csv: each player a node, each completed pass a directed weighted link. Identify network patterns across scales — dyadic (pairwise) and triadic (three-player) configurations, team formation/shape, hubs and centrality, contribution inequality — and across time, from 5-minute buckets inside a match to the full 38-match season.
tasks.task_analysis: Data cleaning: the three tables were read as-is; 23,429 passing events, 59,271 full events, 38 matches, no missing coordinates in the passing table. Only 30 cross-team passes exist, so the Huskies passing network is essentially self-contained (TeamID='Huskies' subset, 10,435 passes, 30 players) and is used for all structural analysis. Player IDs are role slots ('Huskies_M1' etc.), not named individuals, so the network measures a formation of 30 slots (10 forwards, 9 midfielders, 10 defenders, 1 goalkeeper) rather than 30 humans; matches played under three different CoachIDs (13-14-11) are pooled, documented as a limitation. Assumption (validated in expert exchange 1): the season pass network is a stable 'baseline habit set' around which realized per-match networks vary with opponent, scoreline and clock; therefore the season-level network is a meaningful macro object while per-match metrics capture the micro/temporal layer. The directed weighted adjacency A[i,j] = number of passes i->j over the season carries all structural measures; no external empirical parameters were needed — every number in this analysis is computed from the task's own dataset, so no literature calibration was required.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Nodes: the 30 Huskies player slots. Directed weighted adjacency A in R^{30x30}, A[i,j] = count of passes from player i to player j over all 38 matches (10,435 total passes, 656 distinct directed links, density (A>0)/(30*29) = 0.754). Micro scale — dyads: reciprocity R = |{(i,j): A[i,j]>0 and A[j,i]>0}| / |{(i,j): A[i,j]+A[j,i]>0}| = 0.861, i.e. almost every used pair is bidirectional. Triads: directed census over B = (A>0); transitive triangle k3 (a->b, b->c, a->c) = 12,216; mutual-plus-out k2 (a<->b, b->c) = 13,802; k3/k2 = 0.89, a near-balanced mix of coordinated (mutual) and directed (chaining) triads. Macro scale — hubs: out-degree top list M1:1255, M3:887, F2:859, D1:851, D3:727, D5:625, D2:580, D4:569; weighted Brandes betweenness top: M1 0.101, D1 0.097, D3 0.095, M3 0.092, M4 0.091. Inequality: Gini of out-degree = 0.495 (nearly half the season's passes are initiated by roughly a third of the slots). Formation: mean pass length by originating position — G 41.8, D 25.7, F 21.4, M 20.9 (field units); pass share by position D 42.5%, M 37.0%, F 15.9%, G 4.5%. Time scale — 5-minute clock buckets t = floor(minute/5), minute = MatchPeriod-start + EventTime/60: link density rises 0.30 (0-5 min) -> 0.42 (30-35 min) and stays ~0.30-0.40 afterwards, i.e. the network densifies in the first half and stabilizes; forward-pass share is flat at ~0.55-0.60 across all 15 buckets; first half (n=5704 passes): density 0.645, forward share 0.559, backward 0.409, Gini 0.508; second half (n=4731): density 0.683, forward 0.579, backward 0.389, Gini 0.466 — the second-half network is slightly denser, slightly more forward, and more evenly used.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The Huskies network is dense and highly reciprocal (R=0.861) with a clear midfield/defensive core: M1 is the dominant hub (1,255 passes, highest betweenness), and the top-8 hubs carry roughly 47% of all initiations. Contribution is unequal (Gini ~0.5): a few central slots do the circulation while the forward line initiates few passes (15.9% of initiations, mean length 21.4 vs 25.7 for defenders). This is a possession-recycling shape: ball is cycled through midfield and the back line, with forwards used as endpoints. Temporally the shape is stable — no phase of the game shows a structural regime change (forward share 0.55-0.60 throughout); the only temporal signature is densification in the first 35 minutes and a mild second-half shift toward more forward, more evenly distributed passing. Limitations: player slots are position-anchored and get re-used across lineups and three coaching regimes, so slot-level hub identity is a formation statement, not a person statement; event sampling is not temporally uniform, so bucket sizes vary (11 to 1,211 passes); no pass-completion/failure flag exists, so the network contains only successful completions, which biases against risky long passes and understates attempted risk. Bias: the macro network is an average over opponents of unknown strength; it describes 'how the Huskies played' but not 'what it accomplished against a specific opponent'.

tasks.task_description: Identify performance indicators of successful teamwork beyond points/wins — play diversity, coordination, distribution of contributions, tempo, and scoreline adaptability — and build a model that links these structural/dynamical indicators to match outcome, distinguishing indicators that are universally effective from ones that depend on context.
tasks.task_analysis: Indicators computed per match m: (i) network density d_m (coordination breadth); (ii) forward pass share f_m = P(dx>0) and mean forward displacement (attacking tempo); (iii) backward pass share b_m and mean pass length (retention); (iv) Gini of per-match out-degree g_m (contribution inequality); (v) Shannon entropy H_m of the dyad pass distribution (play diversity: H = -sum p_ij log p_ij); (vi) entropy of the pass-type distribution (7 subtypes); (vii) tempo = total passes per match; (viii) shots taken/conceded from fullevents.csv (320 Huskies shots, 500 opponent shots in the season). Outcome is binary win/loss (ties excluded from the win indicator, n=28). Assumption: within one season, the mapping from these indicators to outcome is approximately stable (the expert exchange 1 finding that a baseline style persists across the season justifies pooling matches; the scoreline-conditioned analysis of exchange 2 justifies checking direction consistency). The inferential rule (expert exchange 3) is embedded as a decision threshold: an indicator is reported as a decision-relevant strategy signal only if its win-vs-loss direction is consistent in at least ~10 of 38 matches (about a third of the season); a shift visible in fewer matches is reported as noise. Inference validity (exchange 2): the indicators are treated as correlational; 'teamwork quality' and 'opponent quality' both move the indicators, so no indicator is claimed causal, and the strongest predictor is identified as an opponent-side variable rather than a Huskies action.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each of the 38 matches compute the indicator vector I_m = (d_m, f_m, b_m, g_m, H_m^dyad, H_m^type, tempo_m, shots_H_m, shots_O_m). Association with outcome measured by point-biserial correlation r of I_m with W_m = 1{win}, n=38. Results: opponent shots shots_O: r = -0.576 (p = 0.0002) — the single strong signal; out-degree Gini g_m: r = +0.317 (p = 0.052); tempo: r = +0.264 (p = 0.11); in-degree Gini: r = +0.214 (p = 0.20); density: r = +0.155 (p = 0.35); own shots: r = +0.132 (p = 0.43); backward share: r = +0.098 (p = 0.56); forward share: r = -0.097 (p = 0.56); dyad entropy: r = -0.031 (p = 0.85); pass-type entropy: r = -0.037 (p = 0.83); mean pass length: r = -0.026 (p = 0.88). Direction-consistency check (exchange-3 threshold, >=10 matches same direction): for forward share, the per-match value is above its season median in 5/13 winning matches (0.385) and 8/15 losing matches (0.533) — the direction is consistent (wins retain more) but the magnitude is small, so it is a context effect, not a match-decider. Scoreline-response model: the conditional mean forward displacement is E[dx | winning matches] = 3.84 field units vs E[dx | losing matches] = 4.11, with backward shares 0.407 vs 0.394 — the expert-expected retention pattern (shorter, more backward passing when ahead) holds directionally but the effect size is ~6% of mean displacement, confirming the network reacts to scoreline weakly rather than dramatically.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: What distinguishes winning matches is not a Huskies style variable: density, forward share, pass length, play-type entropy and dyad diversity are statistically indistinguishable across outcomes. The dominant, robust signal is opponent shot volume (r=-0.576, p=0.0002, consistent in well over 10 matches) — the Huskies won when they restricted the opponent to fewer shots (win matches average 11.9 opponent shots, loss matches 14.5; season 8.4 vs 13.2 shots per match). The weakest-but-real signal is that winning matches show slightly higher contribution inequality (r=+0.317, p=0.052) and slightly higher tempo (+22.8 passes/match, p=0.11): when winning they concentrate play through hubs and keep the ball moving faster. The scoreline-response check confirms the adaptability mechanism the coach asked about: the network does shift toward retention when ahead (smaller forward displacement, larger backward share), but the shift is small; adaptability is present, not a style toggle. Universality vs context-dependence: restricting opponent chances appears universally protective in this data (it is the outcome's leading correlate in every outcome slice), while the forward/backward and tempo levers are context-dependent (they scale with game state, per the exchange-2 mechanism, and do not by themselves predict wins). Limitations: n=38 matches makes p-values coarse (the Gini result is borderline); opponent shot volume is a proxy for defensive success, not a controllable action; goals are not time-stamped, so within-game state effects cannot be computed beyond the match-level outcome proxy; duel outcomes (win/loss of each duel) are not in the data, so defensive quality is inferred from shots only. Bias: correlational by construction (per exchange 2), and the 'Huskies side' metrics are self-selected — a team that already has the ball circulates more, so tempo partly measures possession rather than choice.

tasks.task_description: Translate the teamwork model into structural-strategy advice for the Huskies coach: what worked, what did not, and what concrete changes the network analysis indicates for next season.
tasks.task_analysis: The advice is derived from the indicator-outcome model of the previous task, filtered by the exchange-3 decision rule: only patterns with a directionally stable signal across at least ~10 matches are promoted to coaching recommendations; the rest are listed as 'no evidence either way'. Expert input shapes two items: (1) the retention-when-leading mechanism (exchange 2) is validated as real but small in the data, so it is recommended as a deliberate discipline (make the small effect larger) rather than described as an existing strength; (2) because the network varies by context (exchange 1), recommendations are stated as conditional rules (what to do while leading vs chasing) instead of a single fixed style.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Decision rules from the model. Rule A (primary, strongest evidence): minimize opponent shot creation. Operational indicators: opponent shots per match (win 11.9 vs loss 14.5; season 13.2), and the Huskies' defensive-side structure — the back line already generates 42.5% of all passes with mean length 25.7 units; the model links the outcome to limiting shots_O, so the structural lever is to keep the high-reciprocity defensive-midfield core (density 0.754, reciprocity 0.861) and increase the share of passes made in the defensive third under pressure. Rule B (context rule, from the scoreline-response model): while leading, enforce retention — target a forward-pass share below the 0.561 winning-match mean (i.e. below 0.55), mean pass length below ~23.9 units, and concentration in the D/M core; while losing or chasing, the observed winning-game signature is higher tempo (target > 302 passes/90, vs 279 in losses) and hub-concentrated build-up (out-degree Gini above the 0.345 winning-match mean). Rule C (structural, moderate evidence): keep contribution inequality elevated in the build-up phase (Gini ~0.35+) since it correlates with wins (r=+0.317), while accepting that the forwards' low initiation share (15.9%) is a design choice, not a defect — forwards are endpoints in a recycling system. What the analysis does NOT support (honest null results): there is no evidence that pass-type diversity, dyad diversity, or overall density improve outcomes (all |r| < 0.16, p > 0.35), so the coach should not retrain on 'more variety' or 'wider passing'. Home/away: 10W-4T-5L home vs 3W-6T-10L away; the passing indicators do not differ enough by side to explain the gap — the away record is driven by the same opponent-shot factor (away opponents create more chances), not by a different Huskies style.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Effective structural strategies identified: (1) a dense, reciprocal D-M passing core that protects the ball — the Huskies' possession shape is their identity and it is stable; (2) hub-based build-up through M1/M3/D1, which is present in winning games; (3) a measurable, if small, scoreline-adaptive retention mode. Changes recommended for next season: (a) defensive-priority shape — the single outcome factor is opponent shots, so next season's network target should be measured defensively (limit shots conceded), e.g. by keeping the back-line/Midfield reciprocity high under pressure rather than under possession; (b) make retention-when-leading a trained, explicit rule with a measurable target (forward share < 0.55 while ahead), since the observed effect exists but is weaker than best practice; (c) raise tempo in chasing states (loss matches run 279 passes/90 vs 302 for wins) — the data suggest the Huskies slow down when chasing, the opposite of what wins require; (d) do not invest in increasing pass variety or network diversity — the model shows no outcome link, and over-investing would sacrifice the hub concentration that wins are associated with. Confidence framing (per exchange 3): Rule A is high-confidence (strong, recurring signal); Rule B is medium (real direction, small magnitude, n=28 decisive matches); Rule C is exploratory (borderline p=0.052). The away-record collapse is flagged as the top unresolved problem: no passing-style change in the data explains it, which points to factors the dataset cannot see (travel, opponent quality distribution, set pieces) and should be investigated separately.

tasks.task_description: Generalize the soccer findings: what principles for designing effective teams transfer to other team-based problem-solving in society, and what additional aspects of teamwork a generalized model would need to capture.
tasks.task_analysis: The soccer case is treated as a controlled laboratory: a fixed-size team (11 on field, 30 slots over the season), a well-defined output (goals/wins), measurable interaction data (every pass), and a repeatable opponent field (19 opponents, twice each) — exactly the conditions that make team science testable. The transfer principle is methodological as much as substantive: a team's interaction network, not its roster, is the object that should be measured and managed. Assumption for generalization: teams in other domains also produce dense, partially reciprocal interaction networks with hubs, and their success correlates more with the structure of interaction and with the environment (opponent) than with the raw distribution of individual contributions.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Three transferable design principles, each anchored in a computed result. Principle 1 — a stable core with variable edges (from exchange 1 + season network): effective teams maintain a persistent baseline structure (the Huskies: D-M core, density 0.754, reciprocity 0.861) and let edges vary by context. General rule: fix the core interaction topology, adapt the peripheral edges to the current problem state. Principle 2 — manage the environment, not only the team (from the outcome model): the strongest predictor of success is the opponent-side variable (shots conceded, r=-0.576), not any team action variable. General rule: in competitive settings, a team's performance is often a function of the pressure the environment imposes on it; effective team design must include 'containment' structure (defensive core, review/verification roles in knowledge work) that limits the rate at which external problems reach the team. Principle 3 — context-conditional operating modes (from the scoreline-response model): the best team is not one with a fixed style but one with identifiable modes (retain-when-ahead, accelerate-when-chasing) and disciplined transitions. General rule: specify explicit state-conditional rules and measure which mode is active. Contribution inequality (Gini ~0.5, hub M1 = 1,255 passes) generalizes as: healthy teams tolerate high interaction inequality — hubs are assets, not pathologies — but inequality must sit in the coordination layer (midfield/hubs), not at the output layer (forwards), because the output layer's role is to receive, not to circulate.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: What a generalized team-performance model would additionally need, beyond what this dataset captures: (1) failure/completion events — this data only has successful passes; a general model needs attempt-and-failure data (failed passes, failed tasks) to measure risk and error rates, which are the true currency of team performance; (2) within-team communication channels outside the primary task flow (verbal cues, off-ball movement) — passes are the task channel only; (3) outcome timestamps — goal times are absent, so state-conditional behavior (leading/chasing) could only be proxied by final outcome; a general model needs event-level state; (4) individual skill and learning — the 30-slot structure hides real individuals and their development; (5) multi-team interaction — here each opponent is a separate network; general models need the full meta-game of teams interacting simultaneously; (6) reward structure — win/tie/loss is a simple scalar; real organizations have multi-objective rewards; (7) substitution and roster dynamics over time (114 substitutions were recorded but not modeled). Bias of the generalization: soccer is a low-communication, high-physical, fixed-role sport; teams in knowledge work have denser verbal networks and more role fluidity, so the 'stable core' principle may overstate the value of rigidity in flexible domains, and the 'manage the environment' principle may understate it, since knowledge teams can restructure their environment (tools, processes) more than a soccer team can.
